sixtySeconds.whatItDoes: LangChain is a Python framework for building AI agents and apps powered by large language models. It gives you a standard interface for models, embeddings, vector stores and tools, plus a large library of integrations, so you can connect models to your data and swap providers easily.
sixtySeconds.problem: Every model provider and data source has its own API, and wiring them into an app gets messy fast. LangChain provides interoperable components and integrations so you can build and change AI apps without rewriting them.
whoFor: Python developers building LLM apps and agents
Teams connecting models to their own data
Developers who want to switch model providers easily
sixtySeconds.whyChoose: Choose it for the largest integration ecosystem and a standard model interface. For lower-level, controllable agent workflows, its sister project LangGraph is the recommended tool; Deep Agents is a higher-level option.
requirements: An account and API key for the model provider you use

overview: LangChain helps you chain together interoperable components and third-party integrations. Its standard interface covers chat models, embeddings, vector stores, retrievers and tools, so you can swap models in and out as you experiment.

It sits in a wider ecosystem: Deep Agents for agents that plan and use subagents and file systems, LangGraph for low-level agent orchestration, LangSmith for evals, observability and debugging, and LangSmith Deployment for running long-lived agents. A JavaScript version, LangChain.js, is a separate project.
The quickstart is two steps: add the package and initialise a chat model by provider and name. Free courses are available at LangChain Academy. LangChain is MIT licensed.

firstRun.title: Call a chat model
firstRun.code:
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

model = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-5.5")
result = model.invoke("Hello, world!")

steps.title: Initialise a model and invoke it
steps.code:
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

model = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-5.5")
result = model.invoke("Hello, world!")

tutorial.expected: result holds the model's reply. Change the provider and model string to switch models without changing the rest of your code.
